The most commonly performed bariatric procedure is the Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB), the primary topic of this thesis. In Chapter 1, we give a general overview of bariatric surgery, its effects and its complications. In the following chapters the main emphasis is on the postoperative gastrointestinal consequences. In Chapter 2 we study the gastrointestinal symptoms and food intolerance of patients who underwent RYGB two years before. Patients with morbid obesity have more gastrointestinal complaints than normal-weight controls. Therefore, it might be hypothesized that the weight loss after RYGB also leads to a decrease in gastrointestinal symptoms. On the other hand, RYGB is known to sometimes aggravate certain symptoms, for example dysphagia. RYGB also has a strong impact on food tolerance, with many patients developing food intolerance after surgery. Studies with follow- up extending beyond the first year after surgery are scarce, even though it is only in the second year postoperative that the weight loss and eating behavior stabilizes. Therefore, this study was designed to determine the gastrointestinal symptoms and food intolerance in patients two years after RYGB and compare these to an obese control group. The majority of the patients in this control group eventually underwent RYGB as well. In Chapter 3 we study the gastrointestinal complaints of these patients two years after surgery as well. Because of the longitudinal design of this study, we are also able to study the course of gastrointestinal symptoms in time. We can also determine whether patient characteristics, such as preoperative symptoms and prolonged use of medication with abdominal effects such as proton pump inhibitors, can be predictive of the severity of postoperative gastrointestinal symptoms. Considering the routine use of a proton pump inhibitor after RYGB, we study the prevalence of hypomagnesaemia in Chapter 4. Hypomagnesaemia is a rare but sometimes severe complication of proton pump inhibitors. We will determine the prevalence of hypomagnesaemia in the first year of RYGB in a large group of patients, who were routinely prescribed a proton pump inhibitor in the first year after surgery. When a bariatric patient presents with gastrointestinal complaints, it is often difficult for the clinician to distinguish between symptoms indicative of pathology, and functional complaints that need no further evaluation. In Chapter 5 we study three commonly used faecal tests in patients who underwent RYGB. Because RYGB causes 10 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 10 alterations in gastrointestinal anatomy and function, we hypothesize that the levels of these faecal markers might also change. The faecal calprotectin level can be used for the diagnosis or follow-up of inflammatory bowel disease; faecal elastase gives an indication of pancreatic exocrine function; and faecal alpha-1-antitrypsin is a marker for intestinal leakage of protein. In Chapter 6 we study the diagnostic yield of upper endoscopy in patients who underwent RYGB and present with abdominal complaints. An upper endoscopy is frequently performed after RYGB, but often no abnormalities are found. We determine the prevalence of relevant findings at upper endoscopy, such as marginal ulcer and stomal stenosis, in our centre. Next, we aim to identify variables associated with a relevant finding at EGD, and create a prediction model. In Chapter 7 we study endoscopic stent placement in patients with staple line leakage after RYGB or sleeve gastrectomy. Staple line leakage is a severe adverse event of bariatric surgery for which revisional surgery is often necessary. In selected cases, endoscopic placement of a self-expandable stent can be an alternative to surgery. However, stents often migrate, hampering successful treatment or even leading to serious complications. The design of the “Beta stent” is thought to prevent migration; in this chapter we evaluate the success percentage and complication rate of this specific stent. Another complication of bariatric surgery is symptomatic gallstone disease. The rapid weight loss after surgery greatly increases the chance of developing gallstones. However, routine concurrent cholecystectomy was found not to be effective when it comes to costs and comorbidity. Ursodeoxycholic acid was shown to be effective in the prevention of gallstone development, but no studies have been performed with symptomatic gallstone disease as an endpoint. In Chapter 8 we describe the protocol for the UPGRADE, a randomized controlled trial that is currently underway. Finally, in the Summary & General Discussion we will discuss the results of the previous chapters and share our thoughts on their implications and on the future developments in bariatric surgery.

Boerlage TCC, Acherman YIZ, Houweling ST, Holleman F, Gerdes VEA Published in Dutch: Nederlands Tijdschrift voor Geneeskunde 2017;161:D1249. 13 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 13 Abstract Bariatric surgery is performed in patients with a Body Mass Index of >40kg/m2, or >35 kg/m2 with obesity-related comorbidities. The Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and sleeve gastrectomy are the most frequently performed procedures. Patients have 1 lost an average of 25-27% of their weight ten years after surgery, however, there is considerable variation. Obesity-related comorbidities improve or resolve in the majority of cases, most strikingly in type 2 diabetes mellitus and obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome. The prevalence of 30-day complications is less than 5%. Mortality is less than 0.2% in experienced centres. Complications include deficiencies of iron and vitamin B12, gallstone disease and excess skin. The Roux-en-Y gastric bypass has some specific complications such as internal herniation and hypoglycaemia, which are often not recognized. 14 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 14 Case A 41-year-old female consults her general practitioner. Her general practitioner sees her regularly, usually for musculoskeletal complaints and recently with a period of mild depression. Her weight is 133 kg at a length of 174 cm, making a Body Mass Index (BMI) of 44 kg/m2. Recent cardiovascular screening revealed a normal blood pressure, but an elevated fasting plasma glucose of 6.7 mmol/L. She tells that since her teens she has always suffered from obesity. Her weight limits her mobility and she cannot keep up with her children. The “early diabetes” has been decisive for her. An 1 acquaintance has lost 55 kg after a bariatric operation. She wants to grow old healthy and asks her general practitioner whether this type of surgery is an option for her. Indication The indication for bariatric surgery is a BMI of >40 kg/m2, or a BMI of >35 kg/m2 with obesity-related comorbidity such as type 2 diabetes mellitus (DM2), hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome (OSAS), hyperlipidaemia, or arthrosis. The guidelines do not give a clear definition of hyperlipidaemia; we advise to follow the guideline of the national society for general practitioners (‘NHG-standaard’). Further conditions for bariatric surgery are previous successful adherence to a diet and sufficient insight and motivation. (1, 2) Recent studies show good results of bariatric surgery in patients with a BMI of 30-35 kg/m2 and DM2. Although no large randomized trials have been performed, in some countries the guidelines have been adapted to include these patients. In the Netherlands this is currently topic of debate. (3) The age limits are 18 to 65, but in specific cases bariatric surgery can be performed over the age of 65. This is done sporadically in the Netherlands. Bariatric surgery in adolescents younger than 18 is only performed in the setting of clinical trials. Types of surgery The most performed types of bariatric surgery worldwide are the laparoscopic Roux- en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) and the laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy (LSG). (Figure 1a-b) In the Netherlands the majority of operations are RYGB.(4) In the RYGB a small stomach pouch of approximately 30 millilitres is created and connected to the jejunum. This is the alimentary limb through which the food passes. The restrictive effect of the stomach pouch limits the amount of food the patient can eat. The stomach remnant, duodenum and proximal jejunum are connected to the distal jejunum. This way the biliopancreatic limb is created, through which the bile and pancreatic fluids reach the jejunum. Optimal digestion starts only when the food from the alimentary limb (120-150 cm) and the digestive fluids from the biliopancreatic limb mix in the common channel of the jejunum. In the LSG, a large part of the stomach is resected 15 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 15 to create a tube-like stomach consisting of the lesser curvature, creating a restrictive effect. Besides the restrictive effect, both RYGB and LSG cause a stronger feeling of satiety because of the effects of the altered food passage on several gastrointestinal hormones.(5-7) 1 In the early days of bariatric surgery in the Netherlands, gastric banding

starts only when the food from the alimentary limb (120-150 cm) and the digestive fluids from the biliopancreatic limb mix in the common channel of the jejunum. In the LSG, a large part of the stomach is resected 15 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 15 to create a tube-like stomach consisting of the lesser curvature, creating a restrictive effect. Besides the restrictive effect, both RYGB and LSG cause a stronger feeling of satiety because of the effects of the altered food passage on several gastrointestinal hormones.(5-7) 1 In the early days of bariatric surgery in the Netherlands, gastric banding was performed most because of the lower risk of surgical complications. Gastric banding includes the placement of an adjustable synthetic band around the stomach near the cardia. (Figure 1c) Gastric banding is less effective compared to RYGB and LSG when it comes to weight reduction and remission of comorbidities.(8) Patients with a gastric band often develop an unhealthy eating pattern. In response to the obstruction caused by the gastric band these patients develop a diet that consists mostly of easily ingestible high-caloric foods.(9, 10) In the long term almost half of the patients who underwent gastric banding develop complications such as slippage, infusion port malfunction, erosion of the stomach wall or band leakage.(11) As a result, the popularity of gastric banding has decreased in recent years both in the Netherlands and worldwide.(4) Of all patients with a gastric band 20-50% will eventually have the band removed, the majority undergoes conversion to RYGB or LSG.(11-13) There are several types of surgery that create a substantial malabsorption of nutrients by bypassing a greater part of the small intestine, including the distal gastric bypass and the biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch. (Figure 1d) These operations result in more weight loss, but also cause frequent loose stools and in case of incompliance can easily lead to severe deficiencies of protein, calcium and fat-soluble vitamins. In general only patients with a BMI >50 kg/m2 are eligible for these operations. (14, 15) Effects Weight The total weight loss, defined as the percentage of body weight lost in comparison to the preoperative weight, is 32% on average one to two years after RYGB. (16) In the long term the weight increases again in most patients, leading to a total weight loss of 25-27% after ten years.(16, 17) The result in the first years is almost similar for RYGB and LSG.(18) Because the LSG has only been routinely performed as a stand-alone procedure in the last decade, there is a little data on the result in the long term.(19) There is strong variation in the eventual results of a bariatric operation which depend on several, mostly patient-related factors. 16 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 16 1 a b c d Figure 1 a: Roux-en-Y gastric bypass b: Sleeve gastrectomy c: Gastric band d: Duodenal Switch 17 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 17 The mean weight loss after bariatric surgery is less in patients of higher age, ethnic subgroups, or with impaired mobility due to arthrosis of hip or knee.(20-22) Psychiatric conditions can also have a negative impact on the result.(23) The most important predictor however is the postoperative compliance to the new lifestyle that is required, which is difficult to predict beforehand. 1 Diabetes mellitus type 2 The effect of bariatric surgery on the different obesity-related comorbidities is most evident in DM2. After RYGB the insulin response improves almost instantly, independent of the weight loss. This is most likely caused by the incretin-effect. After the meal, nutrients reach the ileum faster and in a less digested state, causing an increased release of incretins from the ileum. These incretins have a stimulating effect on the insulin response by the beta cells of the pancreas.(6) Furthermore, the strongly decreased quantity of food eaten also contributes to the fast improvement in insulin sensitivity. The literature is ambiguous on the effect of the LSG on DM2, but the effect is thought to be less than with RYGB. Therefore, in patients with DM2 the RYGB is usually the preferred procedure.(24, 25) The chance of complete remission of the DM2 after surgery decreases with longer duration of disease and higher preoperative glucose levels.(25, 26) The preoperative BMI has no influence on the likelihood of complete remission. (24, 27) In 46-72% of patients with DM2 the diabetes is in complete remission three years after RYGB, defined as an HbA1c below 6.5% (47 mmol/mol) without medication. Of the patients who were insulin dependent preoperatively, 70-90% discontinued insulin use three years after surgery. (19, 25, 28) There is little data on the effects of the RYGB on DM2 longer than three years after surgery. In 80% of patients who were in complete remission two years after surgery this persists after six years. (29) Other comorbidities

(29) Other comorbidities The systolic blood pressure decreases with a mean of 12 mmHg and the diastolic blood pressure with a mean of 10 mmHg after RYGB or LSG. (30) Three years after RYGB the hypertension is in remission in 30-50% of patients, defined as a blood pressure below target values without medication.(18, 19, 31) OSAS remission, allowing discontinuation of treatment, is achieved in 75% of patients. (32) Three-quarters of the patients with arthrosis of hip or knee experiences improvement in mobility and pain three years after bariatric surgery.(33) Additionally, patients often become eligible for joint prosthesis surgery whereas they were considered unfit prior to bariatric surgery. 18 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 18 Mortality The ten-year mortality of patients undergoing bariatric surgery is almost halved when compared to controls with a similar BMI at baseline. There is a reduction of both cardiovascular mortality and mortality from cancer. (34, 35) The individual patient It can be challenging for the referring physician to determine whether a patient is fit for bariatric surgery. A patient with many obesity-related comorbidities will experience 1 more direct health effects after bariatric surgery. On the other hand, it is often preferable to intervene earlier and prevent the development of these comorbidities. A condition for bariatric surgery is that patients have already done serious attempts to lose weight with conservative measures. Furthermore, a certain comprehension of the surgery and its effects is required. It is important for the referring physician to realize that patients often have unrealistic expectations regarding the result of the operation.(36) The majority of patients will not reach a BMI of <30 kg/m2, let alone <25 kg/m2, after bariatric surgery. In case of an average result the patient described in the case will weigh 100 kg (BMI 33,0 kg/m2) ten years after surgery, although it has to be noted that there is great interindividual variation. Notwithstanding the significant positive effect this average weight loss has on long-term morbidity and mortality, many patients nevertheless hope to reach a BMI <25 kg/m2 despite adequate counselling and can therefore be disappointed in the eventual result. Moreover, patients often express the hope they will be happier after bariatric surgery. The prevalence of depression decreases in the first years after bariatric surgery and the health-related quality of life increases strongly. Five years after surgery the quality of life is still significantly better compared to obese controls. However, the mental health, including the score on the happiness in the SF-36, does not improve in the long term. (37, 38) There is little data on the group of patients that does not experience the desired effects of bariatric surgery. It is just this patient group that is often lost to follow- up, probably causing under-representation in large studies. Our estimate is that less than 10% of patients regret the operation, either because of disappointing results or because of complications or complaints. Complications The short-term complications include the usual surgical complications such as staple line leakage, infection, bleeding and thrombo-embolic events. The combined prevalence of these complications is approximately 5% and is similar for RYGB and 19 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 19 LSG. (39, 40) In experienced bariatric centres the mortality of primary bariatric surgery is <0,2%. (41, 42) Male gender, higher age, higher BMI, smoking and the presence of comorbidities increase the risk of complications. (43, 44) The risk is also higher in revisional surgery after a previous bariatric operation. (45) 1 The most prevalent surgical complications in the first years after surgery are marginal ulcer, stomal stenosis, internal herniation and gallstone disease. The prevalence of marginal ulcer and stomal stenosis varies between 1-5%. (46, 47) The rapid weight loss greatly increases the risk of gallstone development. In the first two years after surgery 8-15% of patients develop symptomatic gallstone disease. (48) The Roux- en-Y construction in RYGB creates two windows in the mesentery, through which small bowel can herniate. This internal herniation usually presents with intermitting, often unspecific abdominal pain. Imaging such as with abdominal CT-scan frequently reveals no abnormalities. Often the diagnosis can only be made by laparoscopy. In case of complete strangulation, small bowel ischemia can develop necessitating emergency surgery. (48) The Roux- en-Y construction in RYGB creates two windows in the mesentery, through which small bowel can herniate. This internal herniation usually presents with intermitting, often unspecific abdominal pain. Imaging such as with abdominal CT-scan frequently reveals no abnormalities. Often the diagnosis can only be made by laparoscopy. In case of complete strangulation, small bowel ischemia can develop necessitating emergency surgery. When the windows are preventively closed during initial RYGB - which is not customary in all centres - the prevalence of internal herniation is 2%.(49) The best known complications in the long term are deficiencies of vitamins and minerals. All patients have to use a multivitamin supplement lifelong. There are many different formulas available, some of which have specifically been designed for bariatric patients. Deficiencies of iron, calcium, vitamin D and vitamin B12 are most prevalent, but in case of therapy incompliance deficiencies of vitamin A, B1, B6, E, K and folic acid and several minerals also occur.(50) There are indications that the prevalence of reflux complaints increases after LSG, but this has yet to be confirmed in large studies.(51) Specific complications of the RYGB are dumping and hypoglycaemia. Dumping is a reaction of the sympathetic nervous system when food is offered to the proximal jejunum too quick or in excessive amounts. Symptoms include transpiration, palpitations, nausea and cramps. Hypoglycaemia is mainly caused by the intake of simple sugars, including fruit juice. In studies with continuous glucose monitoring it was found that the majority of patients after RYGB has hypoglycaemia (glucose < 3.3 mmol/L), usually after meals.(52) This is most likely the result of the previously mentioned incretin-effect and might even be considered a normal response to the altered anatomy. The majority of hypoglycaemic events occur asymptomatically. Patients using a glucose meter sometimes are upset by the low glucose level. It is important to explain to these patients that the physiological feedback mechanisms 20 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 20 ensure rapid correction, so that the hypoglycaemia after RYGB is incomparable to the hypoglycaemia caused by excessive exogenous insulin. A smaller part of patients has symptomatic hypoglycaemia, presenting for example with dizziness or palpitations. These patients often benefit from specific dietary advices, with emphasis on the importance of frequent small meals, eating slowly, and avoidance of “rapid” sugars. (53) Ingestion of fruit sugars or soda is counterproductive because the rapid rise of the blood glucose level evokes a renewed excessive insulin response. When dietary measures have insufficient result, pharmacological treatment with acarbosis 1 can be considered. Acarbosis slows the digestion of carbohydrates from food into monosaccharides, resulting in a more gradual rise of the blood glucose level. In exceptional cases, in which nesidioblastosis (hyperplasia of the beta cells) is involved, treatment with octreotide or surgery can be necessary.(54, 55) Follow-up The current guidelines in the Netherlands require bariatric centres to follow-up on their patients for at least five years after surgery. At the follow-up visits, attention is given to weight, comorbidities and long-term complications and laboratory examination of vitamins and minerals is done. Five years after surgery, the follow-up of patients in a stable situation can be taken over by the general practitioner. Efforts to ensure therapy compliance and annual check-ups, especially of the previously mentioned nutrients for which deficiencies might occur, remain important. Conclusion Patients with morbid obesity despite lifestyle measures should be made aware of the possibility to undergo bariatric surgery. The durable health benefits of a bariatric operation are evident, and the benefits outweigh the drawbacks for most patients. Patients lose approximately 25% of their total body weight in the long term after RYGB or LSG. The ten-year mortality is halved and the majority of patients experience drastic improvement of DM2 and other comorbidities. Nowadays, the surgical mortality is <0.2%. The referring physician should inform the patient about the expected result when it comes to weight loss in the long term. It is important to stress the required lifelong alterations to their diet, the necessary measures to prevent vitamin deficiencies and the possible complications including gallstone disease and excess skin. The RYGB has certain specific complications that are often recognized late, such as hypoglycemia and internal herniation. 21 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 21 In conclusion, the patient described in the case would be eligible for bariatric surgery, with the RYGB most likely the procedure of choice. The weight in the long term will be around 100 kg when an average result is reached, and it is likely that the development of DM2 is prevented. 1 22 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 22 Literature 1. Weight loss does not correlate with total mean GSRS score or the presence of food intolerance. 28 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 28 Introduction The prevalence of obesity and associated comorbidities is increasing. Bariatric surgery is the most effective treatment for morbid obesity in the long term, of which laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (LRYGB) is most commonly performed worldwide.(1, 2) Patients with morbid obesity experience more gastrointestinal complaints than normal-weight controls.(3) Several studies, both longitudinal and cross-sectional, have described the course of gastrointestinal complaints after LRYGB. Most studies show that in the first year after surgery gastrointestinal complaints are slightly better when compared to either the preoperative state or an obese control group. However, some specific complaints such as dysphagia might 2 worsen.(4-7) It is likely that the complaints in the first year postoperative are not representative of the complaints in the longer term, because weight and diet are still changing in this first year.(8) Studies investigating gastrointestinal symptoms longer than 12 months after surgery all have limitations, such as small sample size and high loss to follow-up, which may lead to an underestimation of these symptoms. (9) LRYGB also has a profound influence on food tolerance. Approximately two-third of patients experience food intolerance, with red meat reported most often.(10-12) However, studies on food intolerance generally suffer from the same flaws as the studies concerning gastrointestinal symptoms. This study was designed to investigate gastrointestinal complaints and food intolerance more than two years after LRYGB and compare this to complaints and food intolerance in a pre-bariatric surgery group. Methods A cross-sectional study was performed in a high-volume bariatric centre. All patients who underwent LRYGB from May to October 2012 (a randomly chosen time period) were approached to fill in written questionnaires. In case this was not possible, the questionnaires were administered by e-mail or over the telephone. All patients had a standardized LRYGB with a 4 by 8 cm gastric pouch, 50 cm biliary limb and 150 cm antecolic, antegastric alimentary limb. Both patients with a primary LRYGB and revisional LRYGB after a prior bariatric intervention were included. Due to low numbers the patients who underwent revisional LRYGB were not included in the final analysis. Data of the revisional patients is available in the supplement (Supplement 1; Table S2 - S5). For the control group, consecutive obese patients who fulfilled the criteria for bariatric surgery (a Body Mass Index of >40 kg/m2 or >35 kg/m2 with obesity-related comorbidities) and came to the clinic for preoperative screening were asked to fill in the questionnaires. 29 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 29 Questionnaires The patients had to fill in a general questionnaire, the Gastrointestinal Symptom Rating Scale (GSRS), and a food intolerance questionnaire. The general questionnaire concerned comorbidities, i.e. diabetes mellitus, hypertension and obstructive sleep apnoea syndrome (OSAS), medication use and any medical treatment since the LRYGB. Comorbidities were considered present when self-reporting was confirmed by physical or laboratory examination. Furthermore, characteristics such as height and weight measurements at the outpatient clinic, age, smoking habits and 2 postoperative complications (using the Clavien-Dindo classification to determine severity) were derived from the patient files. The GSRS is a previously validated questionnaire that is specific for gastrointestinal complaints. A revised version was used, because the original GSRS did not contain a question about dysphagia, an important complaint after LRYGB. This version consists of sixteen gastrointestinal symptoms, each is scored on a seven-point Likert scale.(4, 13) The scores on each individual symptom, the total mean score and the scores for symptom clusters are presented. The following clusters were defined: abdominal pain (abdominal pain, hunger pain and nausea); reflux syndrome (heartburn and acid regurgitation), diarrhoea syndrome (diarrhoea, loose stools and urgent need for defecation), indigestion syndrome (borborygmus, abdominal distension, eructation and flatus) and constipation syndrome (constipation, hard stools and feeling of incomplete evacuation).(14) A cluster score was only calculated when all questions in this cluster were answered. A total mean score was calculated when at least 6 questions were answered. The food questionnaire was developed specifically for this study and is therefore not validated (Supplement 2; a Dutch version was administered to the patients). In this questionnaire, patients first answered three questions about whether or not they experience food intolerance, how severe this is and whether it was already present before the gastric bypass. Food intolerance was defined as any adverse event (for example nausea, dumping syndrome or abdominal pain) after ingestion of a certain food type, that caused patients not to eat this food anymore. If patients experienced food intolerance, they chose one or more of the foods from a list of 33 types of food for which food intolerance is known to be common after LRYGB. There

The GSRS scores are presented as medians with 95% confidence interval and interquartile range (IQR) because of non-normal distribution. A comparison was made between the separate, cluster and total mean scores of postoperative patients and obese controls using the Mann-Whitney U test. The correlations between the total score on the GSRS and percentage total weight loss (%TWL) and current BMI, between 2 %TWL and specific symptoms of the GSRS, namely abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting, and dysphagia and between the number of foods for which intolerance was reported and the total mean GSRS score, were determined using Spearman’s rank test. The difference in total mean GSRS score between patients with and without abdominal complications in the first 30 days postoperative, and with and without food intolerance, was determined using the Mann-Whitney U test. The prevalence of food intolerance in postoperative patients and obese controls was compared using the chi-square test. The relation between presence of food intolerance and %TWL and current BMI was tested with the student’s t-test, correlation between number of food intolerances and %TWL and current BMI was determined using the Spearman’s rank test. Several correlations between intolerance for specific food types and specific complaints were hypothesized beforehand: dysphagia and red meat; dysphagia and bread; indigestion cluster and milk. This was determined with subgroup analysis using Mann-Whitney U test. For all analyses, a p of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. No correction for multiple testing was performed because this study was designed to be an exploratory analysis of gastrointestinal complaints. Results Response rates The questionnaire was answered by 294 out of 313 postoperative patients from the predefined cohort, for a response rate of 93.9 per cent. Of the 19 patients who did not fill in the questionnaire, one had died of a non-LRYGB related cause, six were still in follow-up but refused to participate, and twelve patients were lost to follow-up. Of the 294 included patients, 249 underwent primary LRYGB. Forty-five patients underwent revisional LRYGB and are not included in further analyses. The questionnaire was administered in written form by 204 patients, by e-mail in 16 cases and telephonically 31 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 31 in 29 cases. The method of administration of the questionnaire had no significant influence on the total mean GSRS score (p = 0.326) or the presence of food intolerance (p = 0.311). In the preoperative group 318 patients (63.2% of eligible) answered the questionnaire, including 295 patients without previous bariatric surgery, who served as the control group. Discussion This study shows that patients who underwent laparoscopic Roux-en-Y gastric bypass have more gastrointestinal complaints after surgery than similar obese controls at preoperative baseline. Flatulence and borborygmus are most prominent. Food intolerance, especially for food with a high fat or sugar content and for red 2 meat, is a common side effect of LRYGB. There is a positive correlation between gastrointestinal symptoms and food intolerance, but weight loss only correlates weakly with abdominal pain. The results on the general questionnaire confirm findings from previous studies. In the majority of postoperative patients, obesity- related comorbidities were in remission. The high percentage of symptomatic gallstone disease in the first two years after LRYGB is a known effect of weight loss.(16) Patients who underwent gastric bypass surgery had statistically significantly more gastrointestinal complaints than obese controls. Whether all the differences that are statistically significant, are also clinically relevant, can be topic of debate. The individual patient may not notice a small, although statistically significant, overall difference in gastrointestinal complaints. However, the high score on symptoms such as flatulence and borborygmus, is apparent also in clinical practice. Previous publications generally showed a decrease in complaints in the first year postoperatively. Studies with follow-up after the first year are scarce and have methodological limitations, such as small study groups, high loss-to-follow-up, or a cross-sectional design without specifying the original population that the participants were derived from.(6, 17-20) This is important when interpreting the results, for it could very well be that patients with many complaints, or patients who suffer from no complaints at all, have a higher chance of being lost to follow-up. Furthermore, the majority of postoperative patients experience food intolerance, in contrast to obese controls. The food types most often reported were all non-essential, such as fried products and pie. From the more healthy food types, red meat was reported most often. This has been described before and might partly contribute to the high prevalence of iron deficiency after LRYGB.(11) There was a clear positive correlation between food intolerance and gastrointestinal complaints. This seems logical, as the ingestion of food and gastrointestinal function are naturally closely related. There was no correlation between the amount of weight lost and either the total score on 37 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 37 gastrointestinal symptoms or food intolerance. The clinical relevance of the weak positive correlation between weight loss and abdominal pain is unclear. It could be hypothesized that patients who experience more abdominal pain eat less, but further research is needed to confirm this. The results of this study contribute to better knowledge of the long-term effects of LRYGB. This is essential, as it provides a context for clinicians when it comes to the postoperative symptoms that patients experience. Furthermore, it facilitates better preoperative counselling of the patient. Finally, the fact that apart from abdominal pain, gastrointestinal symptoms and food 2 intolerance do not influence weight loss, suggests that other effects of the LRYGB such as alterations in metabolism or increased satiety are more important factors in weight loss. This study has limitations. Because of the cross-sectional design the preoperative and postoperative complaints of the same patient cannot be compared. The food intolerance questionnaire was developed for this study and has not been validated. However, none of the previously published questionnaires about food intolerance has been validated. Some only address a small number of food types, and others are very specific for the eating habits of the country they were developed in. Therefore we felt that the development of a new questionnaire for this study was justified. Strong aspects of this study include the high response rate, the uniformity of the study group regarding duration and methods of follow-up and surgical procedure, and the use of a validated and commonly used gastrointestinal complaints questionnaire, the GSRS. Many previous studies used the GIQLI to assess gastrointestinal complaints. This is however not a symptom-specific questionnaire but determines the influence of symptoms on the quality of life. Future research should include a longitudinal study with follow-up extending more than one year postoperative. The Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) and the sleeve gastrectomy are the most performed bariatric procedures worldwide. (1) Patients with morbid obesity have more gastrointestinal complaints than normal-weight controls. (2) The weight loss after bariatric surgery might alleviate these gastrointestinal complaints, but on the other hand several studies showed that RYGB aggravates certain symptoms. (3-6) Most studies concern the gastrointestinal symptoms in the first year after surgery, but weight and lifestyle are still subject to change in this period. As a consequence the available data on gastrointestinal symptoms will probably not accurately reflect the actual symptoms in the long-term after RYGB. Few longitudinal studies have been performed. One cross-sectional study on gastrointestinal symptoms two years after RYGB showed that patients experience more symptoms and intolerance to specific foods when 3 compared to preoperative controls. (7) However, in this study the gastrointestinal complaints before surgery were not taken into account. Therefore, the current study was designed to evaluate gastrointestinal symptoms and presence of food intolerance before and after RYGB in a large cohort of morbidly obese patients. Methods We performed a prospective cohort study in a high-volume bariatric centre in the Netherlands. Patients undergoing a revisional RYGB after prior bariatric surgery have the same level and distribution of complaints as patients with primary RYGB during follow-up. The most noticeable complaints after RYGB are borborygmus and flatulence. The high prevalence of postoperative food intolerance found in this study confirms the findings from a previous cross-sectional study. (7) There are few longitudinal studies on gastrointestinal complaints after RYGB. Two 3 other studies also found an increase in gastrointestinal symptoms. (4, 10) In a study concerning bowel habits two years after RYGB it was found that more patients experience abdominal pain. (11) The high prevalence of gastrointestinal complaints seems to persist five years after RYGB. (12) In this last study no preoperative data or control group were available but the high scores on the GSRS, especially on the indigestion symptoms, were in line with the findings in our study. The severity of preoperative gastrointestinal complaints is associated with the postoperative symptoms in our study, although the association is not very strong. No prior studies have been published in which this association was investigated. Age was found to be a predictor of postoperative gastrointestinal complaints in a previous study, but this study did not analyse the influence of preoperative symptoms. (4) In our study, age was not a significant predictor. Why gastrointestinal complaints increase after RYGB is not well known. Furthermore, dumping syndrome is a well-known cluster of symptoms after RYGB, including gastrointestinal symptoms. RYGB has several complications that are associated with abdominal complaints, such as internal herniation or gallstone disease. Furthermore, dumping syndrome is a well-known cluster of symptoms after RYGB, including gastrointestinal symptoms. However, many of the gastrointestinal symptoms that occur after RYGB are not evidently linked to a specific complication, and might be related to eating behaviour, changes in intestinal microbiome or psychological factors. (13-15) We found an association between the use of a PPI at the time of questionnaire completion and the severity of postoperative symptoms, and between PPI use and less weight loss. It was reported before that many patients who started a PPI after bariatric surgery continue this in the long term. (16) There is no data on the association between gastrointestinal symptoms and use of a PPI, but it seems logical that patient with more gastrointestinal symptoms are more likely to continue PPI use. It is likely that other medication with effects on the digestive tract, such as laxatives, 58 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 58 mebeverine, loperamide, antiemetics and even opioids, are also associated with postoperative gastrointestinal complaints. However, the number of patients using these drugs was too low to study this. The association between PPI use and less weight loss has been described in a previous study, but this concerned PPI use at the time of bariatric surgery and only weight loss in the first year after surgery was studied. (17) In our study, PPI-users were older than non-users, which could partially explain the difference in %TWL found, as older patients are known to have less weight loss after RYGB. (18) Patients undergoing revisional RYGB had more preoperative complaints than primary RYGB patients. Most of these patients underwent prior gastric banding, which is known to cause more gastrointestinal complaints compared to obese controls. (9) This study has some limitations. Drop-out is a potential source of bias in this study. 3 It is possible that patients with many complaints, or on the contrary no complaints at all, are less likely to answer the questionnaires either because of loss to follow-up or refusal to participate. However, the response rate was high compared to most other studies. (3, 4) Also there was no difference in preoperative gastrointestinal symptoms between patients who did and did not complete the follow-up questionnaires. The number of patients undergoing revisional RYGB was relatively low, which might lead to insufficient power to detect subtle effects in that subgroup. A strong aspect of this study include the high response rate in a uniform study group when it comes to screening methods and surgical procedure. Moreover, the GSRS is a frequently used and validated questionnaire. Finally, this is the first study to investigate the influence of preoperative symptoms on long-term gastrointestinal complaints. In conclusion, this prospective cohort study shows an increase in several gastrointestinal symptoms and in the prevalence of food intolerance after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass for morbid obesity. There is considerable variation between patients however; it is shown that preoperative symptoms and the persistent use of a PPI are associated with the severity of postoperative symptoms. These results contribute to better knowledge of the long-term effects of RYGB, and provide clinicians with a theoretical background for the symptoms their patients experience. Methods Faecal levels of calprotectin, elastase and alpha-1-antitrypsin were determined in 122 patients without signs of gastrointestinal disease one to two years after RYGB. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) is most commonly performed worldwide.(1) RYGB has a restrictive effect on food intake and results in delayed mixing of the food with bile and pancreatic enzymes. RYGB is also known to alter the excretion and plasma concentration of several hormones, the faecal bacterial flora, the absorption of several drugs and patients’ bowel habits. (2-5) Taking these changes in gastrointestinal function after RYGB in account, we hypothesized that the level of faecal markers might also change. This is relevant for several faecal proteins and enzymes that are used to screen for gastrointestinal diseases, or for follow-up of disease severity. Three commonly used fecal tests are calprotectin, pancreatic elastase-1 (elastase) and alpha- 1-antitrypsin (A1AT). A recent article showed significant differences in faecal levels of calprotectin and elastase between seven patients after RYGB and obese controls. (6) Calprotectin is a protein present in most cells, but especially in the neutrophil granulocyte, where it makes up 60% of the cytoplasmic proteins. Neutrophils in the intestinal wall secrete calprotectin in case of intestinal inflammation. It is resistant against proteolysis and after secretion it is not reabsorbed or metabolized in the 5 intestine.(7) Therefore it is excreted in the faeces and can be used to differentiate between inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) and functional complaints with high sensitivity and specificity. It is also used for IBD follow-up.(8) Elastase-1 is a pancreas-specific enzyme secreted by the pancreas for digestion that remains stable and is not reabsorbed throughout the intestinal tract.(9) Determination of elastase in the faeces is a cheap, reliable and non-invasive test, and therefore generally used for diagnosing exocrine pancreatic insufficiency.(10) Secretion of pancreatic juices and bile is regulated by several different gut hormones. The level of faecal alpha-1-antitrypsin was comparable to the general population. Calprotectin The median calprotectin level in our study is 163.5 μg/g, and 87% of patients had a level above the decision limit of <50 μg/g. We believe this influences the validity of the faecal calprotectin test in the RYGB population. When the current decision limit is maintained for patients who underwent RYGB, a high amount of endoscopies will be performed, which might be unnecessary. It is important that clinicians are aware of this. There are several possible explanations for the elevation of faecal calprotectin. We hypothesize that the elevated faecal calprotectin levels after RYGB indicate persistent low-grade inflammation or increased epithelial cell turnover in the gastrointestinal tract. This is supported by the positive correlation with alpha-1-antitrypsin.(7, 18) The location and origin of this possible inflammation is unclear. It is also unknown 80 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 80 whether surgical alterations of the gastrointestinal anatomy other than RYGB also influence the faecal calprotectin level. RYGB causes hyperplasia of the jejunal mucosa of the Roux-limb, but no macroscopic or histologic evidence of inflammation is found in the majority of patients.(14, 22) An increased inflammatory state can be found in the stomach remnant, and more than half of the patients have chronic gastritis in this remnant. (23-25) However, studies in non-RYGB patients with gastritis found no increase in faecal calprotectin.(26) Another option is that inflammation in the biliopancreatic limb causes the elevated calprotectin. There are no studies describing the macroscopic or histologic appearance of this blind loop. Inflammation in this part of the intestine could be due to the deleterious effect of bile acids and pancreatic enzymes. These are not buffered by ingested food, as would happen in the normal anatomy, and are known to cause damage to the enterocytes.(27) Inflammation might also be caused by bacterial overgrowth in the stomach remnant

gastritis in this remnant. (23-25) However, studies in non-RYGB patients with gastritis found no increase in faecal calprotectin.(26) Another option is that inflammation in the biliopancreatic limb causes the elevated calprotectin. There are no studies describing the macroscopic or histologic appearance of this blind loop. Inflammation in this part of the intestine could be due to the deleterious effect of bile acids and pancreatic enzymes. These are not buffered by ingested food, as would happen in the normal anatomy, and are known to cause damage to the enterocytes.(27) Inflammation might also be caused by bacterial overgrowth in the stomach remnant or the biliopancreatic limb.(28) In non-RYGB patients, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth did not cause an increase in faecal calprotectin,(29) but other studies showed that the faecal calprotectin level can change when there are significant changes in gut microbiota. (30) The colon does not seem the most likely location for the increased calprotectin excretion, as its anatomy is not altered in RYGB. However, there are persistent pro- inflammatory changes in the rectum after RYGB.(31) It is possible that the elevation of faecal calprotectin is a sign of low-grade colonic inflammation, in line with these 5 findings. We feel that methodological errors are unlikely. Calprotectin was collected and stored according to current standards. It is known to remain stable for several days at room temperature, and longer when frozen.(7) All faecal tests were done in one batch by the same experienced laboratory. All patients had undergone surgery at least one year prior to inclusion and had no severe gastrointestinal complaints. Strict exclusion criteria were set for major factors that influence calprotectin levels, but not for factors such as age, fibre intake and physical activity that are known to have only minimal influence. (32, 33) PPI and NSAID use can influence calprotectin, therefore these drugs were discontinued for at least three days prior to faeces collection. Subgroup analysis of patients who discontinued the PPI for 3-7 days versus those who had stopped PPI use for more than 7 days before collection, revealed no significant difference in faecal calprotectin levels. Only five patients occasionally used NSAIDs prior to faeces collection. Calprotectin level in these patients did not differ from patients who never used NSAIDs. Furthermore, calprotectin levels did not correlate with the current BMI, percentage total weight loss or age in this study. The determination of a new decision limit for calprotectin after RYGB is not possible 81 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 81 based on this study. A large cohort of RYGB patients diagnosed postoperatively with IBD would be needed for this. In practice, when the prevalence of IBD is taken into account, this is not a feasible study design. Elastase The median faecal elastase level is lower in patients after RYGB than in the general population, as was also found in a previous study.(6) However, the majority of patients had a level above the limit for pancreatic insufficiency. None of the 16 patients (13%) with a faecal elastase level below the reference value had clinical or biochemical evidence of pancreatic insufficiency. Therefore it is possible that the specificity after RYGB is lower than the known specificity of 90-93% in the general population.(10) This can only be confirmed by performing invasive pancreatic function tests in these patients, which was not done in the course of this study. There was evidently no correlation between faecal calprotectin and elastase in this study, contrary to previous findings.(6, 34) This may be explained by a smaller study group and the selection of patients with pancreatic diseases in these previous studies. No comparison is possible with preoperative faecal values of the participants due to the cross-sectional design. However, we deem it unlikely that all patients already had elevated calprotectin levels before surgery as these patients had no gastrointestinal disease prior to RYGB. Previous studies concerning calprotectin levels in obese patients never showed levels as high as observed in this study.(17, 33) Second, no endoscopy, invasive pancreatic function tests or radiological examinations were performed in this study. However, often no abnormalities are found. This study aimed to investigate the incidence of relevant findings at upper endoscopy and identify patient characteristics associated with a relevant finding. Methods A retrospective cohort study was performed. All patients presenting with abdominal complaints after LRYGB who consequently underwent a diagnostic upper endoscopy were identified from a prospective endoscopic database. Primary outcomes were the number and type of relevant findings at upper endoscopy and the association between patient characteristics and a relevant finding. Associations were assessed by univariable and multivariable logistic regression. Relevant findings were defined as abnormalities requiring treatment. Results The study population consisted of 250 patients, of which 98 (39.2%) had a relevant finding at upper endoscopy, mostly marginal ulcer and stomal stenosis. Sex (OR for 6 female 0.29 (0.09-0.90)), alcohol consumption (OR 7.27 (1.58-33.36)), dysphagia or suspicion of bleeding as reason for upper endoscopy (OR 3.62 (1.54-8.52) and 39.93 (4.96-321.47) respectively, when compared to abdominal pain as referral reason), an abnormal upper gastrointestinal series (OR 6.81 (2.06-22.48)) and no abdominal ultrasound (OR 7.41 (1.48-37.08) compared to a normal ultrasound) were significantly associated with a relevant finding at upper endoscopy. The final model had an area under the curve of 0.838 (95% CI 0.786-0.890). Conclusions In this study we found that sex, alcohol consumption, referral reason and prior imaging studies are associated with the chance of a relevant finding at upper endoscopy after LRYGB. (9) Marginal ulcer has a mean incidence of 4.6% after LRYGB, but this can be as low as <1% in some series.(10) It is most prevalent in the first year after surgery, with a mean time between surgery and first symptoms of approximately 4 months.(10) Stomal stenosis has a prevalence of 3.1 to 7.8 %, and is most prevalent in the first 3 months after surgery.(11, 12) Because of the high number of upper endoscopies without a relevant finding, it would be useful if patients could be selected to undergo upper endoscopy based 6 on clinical or demographic characteristics. However, only few studies evaluated patient characteristics that are associated with relevant findings at upper endoscopy. Additionally, these studies evaluated only a small number of variables, had a relatively small sample size, or concerned open surgery.(7-9) The current study aimed to evaluate the number and type of relevant findings after upper endoscopy in a large cohort of patients who underwent LRYGB and to identify patient characteristics that are associated with a relevant finding at upper endoscopy. Methods Setting and study population This study was performed in a high-volume bariatric centre of excellence, where bariatric surgery is done since 2007. For LRYGB a standardized procedure with a 30 ml gastric pouch, a 50 cm biliary limb, and a 150 cm alimentary limb was used. Postoperatively, patients in this cohort were advised to use a proton pump inhibitor 89 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 89 (PPI) for one year and received regular follow-up for at least five years. An upper endoscopy was only performed in case of upper gastrointestinal complaints. All upper endoscopies performed after LRYGB, either primary or revisional, between 2007 and July 2015 were retrieved from the endoscopy database (Endobase, Olympus Europe, Hamburg, Germany) and linked with our prospectively maintained database of bariatric procedures. This way all patients who underwent upper endoscopy in our centre following bariatric surgery were identified. We excluded patients who underwent a therapeutic endoscopy, such as placement of a nasojejunal feeding tube or implantation of an endoscopic stent for confirmed anastomotic leakage. Additionally, patients who underwent LRYGB elsewhere, or underwent an upper endoscopy unrelated to LRYGB, for example follow-up of Barrett’s oesophagus, were excluded. In case a patient underwent multiple endoscopies after LRYGB, only the first endoscopy was included. Variables that were hypothesized to be associated with a relevant finding at upper endoscopy were retrieved from the database. This included sex, age at time of surgery, history of abdominal surgery and primary or revisional LRYGB. Furthermore, the following variables were determined at time of upper endoscopy: hypertension, diabetes, NSAID use, use of inhaled corticosteroids, proton pump inhibitor use, smoking (>1 cigarette a day in the last week), alcohol (> 1 unit per week) use, 6 percentage total weight loss (%TWL), time after surgery and the referral reason for upper endoscopy. The referral reason noted by the referring physician and by the endoscopist was compared and in case of discrepancy the referral reason was determined by two researchers (T.B. and P.W.) and discussed until consensus was reached. Four referral groups were created. The group “abdominal pain” consisted of pyrosis and pain. The groups “dysphagia” and “nausea or vomiting” consisted of these symptoms only. Patients referred for suspicion of bleeding or leakage were combined in one group because separate groups had insufficient numbers to perform multivariable analysis. Finally, imaging studies prior to upper endoscopy were included: CT-scan of the abdomen, abdominal ultrasound, upper gastrointestinal series and plain abdominal X-ray. For this retrospective cohort study, no formal ethical review was necessary according to the Dutch act on medical research with human subjects (WMO). Relevant findings were defined as abnormalities or considered to be the cause of the complaints the 90 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 90 patient presented with, or abnormalities requiring any type of treatment. Predefined relevant findings were: marginal ulcer (i.e. an ulcer at the gastrojejunal anastomosis); stomal stenosis, defined as a stricture requiring endoscopic dilatation; bleeding, defined as haemorrhage from the upper gastrointestinal tract for which an intervention was necessary; reflux oesophagitis; Candida oesophagitis; gastrogastric fistula; anastomotic leakage; and food impaction. Findings without clinical relevance, such as a visible suture or staple without inflammation or narrowing of the lumen, were not included. Secondary outcomes were individual relevant findings. Statistical methods For continuous variables mean and standard deviation are given in case of normal distribution and median and interquartile range (IQR) in case of non-normal distribution. For categorical variables numbers and percentages are given. The association between the occurrence of a relevant finding at upper endoscopy and patient characteristics was first explored using univariable logistic regression. Results are presented as odds ratio (OR) with 95% confidence interval (95% CI). When calculation of an OR and p-value was not possible with logistic regression due to 0 cases in any outcome, the OR was calculated by adding 0.5 to each outcome and for statistical significance testing Fisher’s exact test was used. These variables were excluded from multivariable analysis. Variables with a p-value <0.5 at univariable analysis were then included in a multivariable logistic regression model (full model). By means of stepwise backward selection variables with a p>0.05 were eliminated from the model (final model). A detailed description of the final model is available 6 in the supplement. Separate analyses were performed in which only the patients with marginal ulcer were compared to the patients without a relevant finding at upper endoscopy, and for patients with stomal stenosis versus those without a relevant finding. To assess the influence of inclusion of imaging studies, the multivariable logistic regression analysis was also performed for the primary outcome without imaging studies. The same statistical procedures were applied. A p-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant. SPSS Statistics software packages version 21 (Chicago, Illinois) was used for statistical analysis. Eight findings were diagnosed only once, including anastomotic leakage, an ulcer other than a marginal ulcer, and a gastrogastric fistula. The results of the univariable and multivariable analysis examining factors associated with a relevant finding at upper endoscopy are shown in table 2. In the univariable analysis male sex, revisional LRYGB, alcohol consumption, dysphagia and suspected bleeding or leakage as reason for referral, abnormal upper gastrointestinal series, no abdominal ultrasound prior to upper endoscopy, no abdominal CT-scan prior to upper endoscopy, shorter time between surgery and upper endoscopy, and lower %TWL were significantly associated with a relevant finding at upper endoscopy. The association between time after surgery and outcome of upper endoscopy is shown in figure 1. Furthermore, in several other studies different surgical techniques were used, such as open instead of laparoscopic surgery. Finally, alcohol use is notoriously difficult to assess, especially in a retrospective study design. An association between shorter time after surgery and a relevant finding at upper endoscopy was described in previous studies.(7-9) This association was found in our study too, but only at univariable analysis. After multivariable analysis, shorter time after surgery remained positively associated with stomal stenosis and marginal ulcer, but not for all relevant findings together. This discrepancy is most likely explained by the patients with esophagitis in the combined group. These patients form a relatively small subgroup but generally presented long after surgery. 98 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 98 The inclusion of imaging studies in the multivariable model might be topic of debate. We are aware that this might introduce overlap in the model because baseline characteristics might also influence the decision to request imaging studies. However, it was decided to include these studies because in clinical practice, these often influence the decision whether or not to refer for upper endoscopy. A study excluding these imaging studies would therefore not be representative of the actual clinical situation. Although ultrasound is not a suitable procedure to diagnose stomal stenosis or marginal ulcer, it was hypothesized the clinician’s decision might be influenced by the result. For example, when gallstones are found at ultrasound in a patient with unspecific abdominal pain, this can be assumed to be the cause, and no upper endoscopy is performed. The fact that the absence of an ultrasound, rather than the presence of abnormalities at ultrasound, was associated with a relevant finding at upper endoscopy might indicate that the patients who underwent an ultrasound presented with complaints that were more difficult to interpret. Abnormal upper gastrointestinal series were also correlated with relevant findings at upper endoscopy, mostly due to the high positive predictive value for stomal stenosis. Besides the previously mentioned association with shorter time after surgery, alcohol use and referral reason, presence of a marginal ulcer was also associated with use of an NSAID, not using a PPI and smoking. These are all previously established risk factors for marginal ulcer.(10, 17) Inhaled corticosteroid use did not influence the risk of a relevant finding at upper endoscopy in our study, although it is reported 6 that corticosteroids increase the risk of a marginal ulcer.(18, 19) Possibly, there has already been a preselection in patients referred for upper endoscopy in this study, or the number of patients using corticosteroids in our cohort was too low to detect a significant difference. Helicobacter pylori infection was not included as a variable in this study because infection with Helicobacter pylori is routinely tested and eradicated prior to surgery in our centre. In addition, previous studies have shown that Helicobacter pylori is not associated with marginal ulcer development.(10) Shorter time between surgery and onset of symptoms, an abnormal upper gastrointestinal series and dysphagia as reason for referral were associated with stomal stenosis. This is in line with the results from previous studies, which showed that stomal stenosis generally occurred within the first three months after surgery, and upper gastrointestinal series have a high diagnostic yield.(9, 14) One study evaluated variables associated with stomal stenosis specifically. In this study, age and gastro- oesophageal reflux disease were predictors of stomal stenosis.(20) The influence of 99 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 99 preoperative gastro-oesophageal reflux disease could not be evaluated in our study because no routine preoperative upper endoscopy is performed in our centre. This is the largest study in which variables associated with relevant endoscopic findings after LRYGB are studied. We present a homogenous cohort when it comes to surgical and endoscopic technique and follow-up program, in a bariatric centre of excellence. Because multivariable analysis was performed in this study, it becomes clear that several previously reported associations are interrelated. For example the correlations between time after surgery and relevant findings at upper endoscopy, and between relevant findings and dysphagia as presenting symptom, are partly due to the early presentation of stomal stenosis. Although this is the largest cohort currently known for this study objective, the number of patients in the subgroup analyses is still relatively small. Therefore, the numbers for some variables might not be large enough to reach statistical significance. Furthermore, although patients with suspicion of leakage were included, this diagnosis is often made on imaging studies and an upper endoscopy is not always performed. 6 In the interpretation of the study results it should be realized that this study was designed to advise endoscopists on whether or not to perform an upper endoscopy in case of gastrointestinal complaints after LRYGB. In addition, it concerns a selected population, namely those patients referred for upper endoscopy. Therefore, no conclusions can be drawn about the risk factors for development of an anastomotic complication in the general LRYGB population. Finally, the results should be confirmed in a prospective study before these factors can be used as predictors in clinical practice. In conclusion, this study identified several factors associated with a relevant finding at upper endoscopy after LRYGB, of which the referral reason, prior imaging studies, gender and alcohol use are most notable. (5) Endoscopically placed self-expandable stents can be an alternative to surgery in selected cases when there is relatively limited leakage, or when leakage persists despite revisional surgery. Stent placement is effective in more than 50% of these selected cases.(6) The most frequent adverse event of stent placement in patients after bariatric surgery is migration with a prevalence varying from 4.8 - 67%, depending on stent type and indication for placement.(6-8) The Niti-S BetaTM stent (TaeWoong medical, South Korea) is an over-the-wire nitinol stent, which is specifically designed for the treatment of staple line leakage after bariatric surgery. It has a flange at the proximal end and the proximal part of the stent is thickened by means of a silicone covered double stent layer, creating a double- bump (Figure 1). It is stated that the double-bump prevents migration by increasing the radial pressure, but there are no clinical or experimental data supporting this. The present study was designed to evaluate the success and adverse event rate of the Niti-S Beta stent. Methods 7 A retrospective study was performed in three high-volume bariatric centres (each > 800 bariatric interventions annually) in the Netherlands. The endoscopy database in each centre was searched for all consecutive patients who underwent placement of a Niti-S Beta stent for staple line leakage after bariatric surgery. The medical ethics committee certified that formal ethical review was not necessary for this study. Stent procedure The Niti-S Beta stent is a self-expandable fully covered double-bump metal stent with radiopaque markers at both ends. All stents were placed by endoscopists with experience in stent placement. The indication and timing of stent placement and the type and size of the stent were at the discretion of the local surgeon and endoscopist. 111 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 111 The length of the stents ranged from 100 to 180 mm and the inner diameter from 20 to 28 mm. The location and size of the leak were determined endoscopically and marked with an external radio-opaque marker if preferred by the endoscopist. Next, a guidewire was placed through the scope in the duodenum or proximal jejunum. The scope was removed and the delivery device (20 to 22 Fr, length 70 cm) was introduced over the guidewire. The stent was placed under fluoroscopic guidance and/or endoscopic guidance at the discretion of the endoscopist. The stent was positioned so that the leak was in between the two bumps. After placement, the location was checked by fluoroscopy and endoscopic visualization. If necessary the stent was relocated. The day after stent placement, an upper gastrointestinal series or oral methylene blue test was performed to assess potential persisting leakage. In general, oral intake was started after proof of the absence of significant leakage. Timing of removal of the stent was determined by the endoscopist in discussion with the surgeon. The stent was removed using an endoscopic forceps grasping the proximal or distal retrieval string. Imaging was only repeated in case of suspicion of persisting or recurrent leakage. Imaging was only repeated in case of suspicion of persisting or recurrent leakage. Outcome measures The primary outcome was resolution of the leakage. Resolution was defined as closure of the leak (confirmed by endoscopic visualization of the leak or radiographic imaging with oral contrast) within one week after stent removal without signs of a recurrent leak after 6 weeks of follow-up and without need for additional surgical or endoscopic intervention. Secondary outcomes were adverse events of stent placement. Predefined adverse events were migration, fixation complicating removal, stenosis, 7 bleeding and complaints of pain or dysphagia due to the stent and unresponsive to medical treatment. Migration was defined as dislocation of the stent requiring an additional procedure, either endoscopic or surgical, to remove or reposition the stent. Fixation was defined as overgrowth of tissue at the stent margins hindering endoscopic removal and necessitating an additional (endoscopic) procedure for removal. Stenosis was defined as a stricture requiring endoscopic dilatation. Bleeding was defined as symptomatic gastrointestinal haemorrhage requiring a therapeutic intervention. Statistical analysis For the primary outcome a per-patient analysis was performed. Adverse events were analysed per-stent and per-patient. Data extracted included demographics, medical history and medication use, type of bariatric surgery, time to stent placement, concurrent interventions, stent size, duration of treatment, reason for stent removal, 112 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 112 adverse events and outcome. Descriptive statistics were used for all data, with mean and standard deviation (SD) in case of normal distribution, and median and range for non-normal distribution. For the main outcomes, proportions and percentages are shown. Several factors associated with success were hypothesized beforehand. The differences in success and adverse event rate between stents placed as initial treatment versus stents after failed revisional surgery, first versus consecutive stents, and LRYGB versus LSG, were calculated with the chi-square test. Potential influence of time between initial surgery and stent implantation on successful resolution was checked using the Mann-Whitney U test. Results Thirty-eight patients were included, who underwent 50 stent placements in total. The first stent was placed in October 2009. The supplier of the stent (Prion Medical BV) confirmed that, from October 2009 to March 2016, 50 stents were provided to the participating centres. Thus all consecutive stent placements during the entire study period have been included. Patient characteristics are shown in table 1. Patients had a mean age of 45 and a mean BMI of 43.0 kg/m2. This study shows that staple line leakage after bariatric surgery can be effectively treated with the Beta stent in 66% of cases. In a recently published series, with 10 patients who had staple line leakage after LSG, the success rate of the Beta stent was 80%.(13) This success rate seems comparable to the results of other stents in previous studies, which ranges from 62 - 96%.(7, 8, 10-12, 14-19) However, comparison is hampered because all studies, including this study, are retrospective in nature and therefore subject to selection bias. In addition, there are differences in indication, definition of success and stent type between studies. For example, in the study describing the highest success rate (96%) a partially covered metal stent was placed in all patients with staple line leakage, including small leaks that might also have closed with conservative management only.(15) The definition of success in our study was stricter than in some other studies. Four patients who had resolution of the leakage more than one week after stent removal, but without additional interventions, were not considered successful in this study. If these patients had been defined as successful, as in several other studies, the success rate would have been higher (76%). The most striking factor associated with success in this study was the difference 7 between stents placed as initial treatment (group 1) versus those placed after failed revisional surgery (group 2). In group 1 the success rate was 100%, compared to 55% success rate in group 2. This result raises the question whether immediate stent placement should be considered in all patients with staple line leakage.(15) However, it must be underlined that the difference between the two groups in this study is subject to considerable bias. Stent placement was mostly the initial treatment in patients with only minor leakage. In contrast, leaks that persist after revisional surgery are generally larger and more difficult to close. Therefore the chance of successful stent treatment in these cases may be lower. Time between initial bariatric surgery and stent placement was not a predictor of success in this study. This is in contrast to previous studies, where stent placement early after surgery increased the chance of successful leak resolution.(10, 14) This variation between studies is most likely due to selection bias, with differences 118 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 118 in indication and timing of stent placement between studies. Whether early stent placement does or does not increase the success rate should be subject of further prospective research. In previous studies, placement of a consecutive stent when the first stent failed to resolve the leakage was feasible and had a considerable success rate.(6) The chance of success of a consecutive stent did also not differ from the first stent in our series. This confirms that placement of a consecutive stent should be considered when the first stent has failed to resolve the leakage. The most frequent adverse event of stent placement is migration.(6-8) Despite the novel double-bump structure of the Beta stent, which has specifically been designed to prevent migration, migration occurred in 32% of patients (26% of stents) in this study. This seems comparable to the results of other fully covered stents, with a migration rate of 18 - 67% in previous studies.(8, 11, 16, 17, 19, 20) Partially covered stents are less prone to migration with a migration rate of 5 - 15%.(7, 10, 14, 15, 18) However, these stents are often difficult to remove.(7) Several options to prevent migration of fully covered stents have been described. Two studies describe fixation of the stent by endoscopic clipping, but only a small number of patients with staple line leakage was included.(21, 22) Some authors advocate suturing of the stent to the oesophageal wall to prevent migration. However, migration rate was still 33% in one study.(23) In this study, there was one death unrelated to the procedure and no stent-related deaths. However, there was one life-threatening adverse event: haemorrhage from an aorto-esophageal fistula caused by mechanical pressure of the stent. In previous 7 studies mortality was described as well, most often not stent-related.(5, 7, 8, 24) Stent-related deaths, due to perforation or bleeding, were described in two studies. (10, 19) In one study, a fatal bleeding was caused by the mechanical pressure of the stent, which caused the bleeding in this study too.(19) Therefore, this adverse event does not seem to be unique for the Beta stent. However, the double-bump structure of the stent leads to increased mechanical pressure at the level of the two proximal bumps on the oesophagus, which may increase the risk of eroding adverse events such as happened in this case. Alternative endoscopic treatment options for staple line leakage include over-the- scope clipping, overstitching of the leak in case of small leaks, endoluminal vacuum therapy, or drainage with a pigtail.(25-28) However, due to the small number of 119 524098-L-bw-Boerlage Processed on: 20-9-2018 PDF page: 119 patients in these studies and the lack of prospective studies and studies comparing different treatment options, it is yet unclear which treatment option has the highest chance of success. The main limitation of this study is the retrospective design, which has led to a selection bias. The multicentre design is both a strength and a limitation of this study. There existed small differences in the indication for stent placement between the participating centres. However, the technique for placement was comparable between centres. In conclusion, placement of the Niti-S Beta stent for staple line leakage after bariatric surgery is feasible and the results seem to be similar to other stents. This study does not support the statement that the double-bump structure prevents migration.
